messages.subject: Distance stratification question
parts:
Russ,

I'm forwarding your question to the distance-sampling list to see if anyone
else wants to take a stab at addressing it (I'm quite busy at present). Let
me know in a couple of days if no-one else answers and I'll have a go. If
you do get some replies, perhaps you could collate or summarize them to the
list.

All the best,

- Len

me!

Hi Len-

[...]

Okay Len, I don't want to impose, but I have a larger question regarding
stratification\post-stratification. If you feel this is more appropriate for
the list or others, feel free to forward. And though I've no wish to waste
your time, I'd be delighted to discover this is a trivial question.

I have the task of producing annual density estimates for over 120 bird
species at the following spatial scales: statewide, by physiographic region,
and by study site (though estimates by site by year are not expected to be
reliable). We have data on about 270 species, but only about 120 have
comfortably more than 80 total observations. There are 7 years of data (soon
to be 8 if I don't hurry), 4 physiographic regions, and 32 study sites. The
4 physiographic regions have from 1 to 14 study sites (see attached graphic
[Len says: I copied this to
http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distance/images/utahbird.jpg so you can use
your browser to see it]). Each study site has 10 point transects and is
surveyed twice per season. The study site is the sampling unit. The 10
point transects comprising each study site are treated as sub-samples, and
the two visits per year are treated as replicates (i.e., Survey Effort = 2,
or 1 if missing one visit: there are 7 visits completely missing out of the
224 total. Sub-question: should I be using Survey Effort = 20 instead of 2?
If this is a reasonable approach, i.e., would not shift analysis emphasis
from the site to the point, inflate sample sizes, nor deflate density
estimates; it would allow me to account for the 15 visits that over the years
missed one to several points. If doing so would make the point the sampling
unit instead of the site, how then would distance handle a Survey Effort of,
say, 1.7, corresponding to a year in which one of the two visits to a site
only managed 7 of the 10 points?). The data for each species is split out
and analyzed separately.

Given the stratification limitations of Distance 3.5, how do I arrange my
data so as to avoid spurious results while making the most out of the sample
size? The question boils down (I think) to whether or not each year's data
from a given site can/should be considered statistically independent from the
other years. Biologically, I can see arguments for both sides: site fidelity
and similar vegetation structure vs. high turnover/mortality rates plus
variable territory size and shape, but I lean toward independence (also, 5
years of banding data at a couple sites shows about 10% or less site fidelity
per year). Statistically, I lean toward caution. Being of two minds, I
prepared and analyzed my data both ways since a) the book recommends
stratifying by area and post-stratifying by time, but b) my initial data
explorations found year effects to be much larger than physiographic region
effects. Analysis results for American Robins from both sort orders are in
the two zipped project files "AMROYEAR" (Year/Site/Phys sort order) and
"AMROPHYS" (Phys/Site/Year sort order). Unfortunately the results are quite
different, but both seemingly plausible. Plus, both are also quite different
from the pattern seen in a 'traditional' relative abundance analysis I did
for comparison's sake.

Any suggestions? Many thanks

-Russ
